display_title: The proposed method is quite a lot like mixtures of experts, and this needs to be addressed

content.title: The proposed method is quite a lot like mixtures of experts, and this needs to be addressed
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.review:
The manuscript aims to improve the performance of neural networks on small datasets, by using an ensemble approach to reduce the variance.  This is a worthy goal, and the overall approach of using an ensemble method makes sense, based on the variance-reducing properties of bagging.  Postive results are reported on two datasets, indicating that the method may work as intended.  The experiments varying the size of the training set are also useful for exploring the authors' hypothesis.  It is appreciated that the authors made their code available.

However, while the proposed ideas are interesting, there are concerns about the novelty in relation to a long line of previous work.  The approach assigns weights that sum to one for each instance, where the weights associate that instance with different models, and these weights are updated via an iterative procedure.  Thus, each model is allowed to specialize on a subset of the data, according to the weights.  This should immediately bring to mind the notion of a mixture model, trained via EM.  Indeed, the mixture of experts model of Jacobs et al., dating back to 1991, does exactly this in a supervised learning context, as is studied here.  This type of model has been extensively studied for well over two decades:

Jacobs, R. A., Jordan, M. I., Nowlan, S. J., & Hinton, G. E. (1991). Adaptive mixtures of local experts. Neural computation, 3(1), 79-87.
Yuksel, S. E., Wilson, J. N., & Gader, P. D. (2012). Twenty years of mixture of experts. IEEE transactions on neural networks and learning systems, 23(8), 1177-1193.

I am unsure of whether the proposed updates, which are suggested heuristically, will exactly correspond to the EM algorithm for mixtures of experts (MoE).  Regardless, they are very closely related, and this needs to be addressed in the manuscript.  If they are different, the paper must demonstrate that the approach has superior performance to MoE.  If they are not, the novelty of the paper is greatly reduced, although this may help to justify the proposed approach, and could lead to new analyses.  Mixtures of experts have a model-based theoretical basis, while the present work is heuristically motivated.

Only two datasets are used in the experiments, which leaves questions on whether the results will generalize to other datasets.  Results on at least one more dataset would greatly strengthen confidence in the results.

To summarize, while the manuscript has some interesting ideas, the relationship to a long line of previous work, the mixture of experts model, is not properly addressed, which means that the paper cannot presently be accepted in its current form.  The experimental results need to be extended, as comparisons to mixtures of experts are important to include (even if the proposed approach ends up being different to that work), and only two datasets are used.  The lack of theoretical justification of the proposed approach becomes more of a concern in light of the fact that its primary competitor, mixtures of experts, has a model-based justification.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: A method for building complementary networks - interesting, but many foundational questions haven't been addreesed

content.title: A method for building complementary networks - interesting, but many foundational questions haven't been addreesed
content.review:
This paper proposes an iterative method to computing complementary weights between two networks for small datasets.

All in all, there might be something interesting in this topic, but since there's no theoretical analysis and background in the paper, it's not clear why this method should work or be better than others.

Comments:
- On the theoretical front, I'm not sure what is it that is being optimised by the iterative complementary reweighting updates. What is the loss function? What would the best two models? 
- Why is the reweighting only reliant on the posteriors rather than on mistakes (i.e. labels are not being used at all in the computation of sample weights, only the posterior)? 
- Why not to ensemble all the models up the end for the prediction (i.e. what is so special about the last models that you want to only keep them - this relates to the question about what is it that is being optimised)?
- Since the application is computer vision here, the question is that why not to use/compare to CNNs for this task?
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: interesting idea but experiments not convincing enough
content.review:
This paper proposes interactive boosting to train two complimentary networks for relative small image classification. This is an interesting idea for small sample training, although I am not sure whether it can be applied to "really"  small sample datasets since UIUC or LabelMe contains at least thousands of images.  

The experimental results are not very convincing, and I wish the final paper could compare with more baselines, including
1. adapting pretrained model (e.g., from ImageNet) to the proposed problem
2. deep CNN with dropout 
3. deep CNN with distillation
4. deep CNN with data augmentation
which all are popular techniques to apply deep network for small sample problems.

content.title: Findings based on the reproducing of the paper
content.comment:
We reproduced the primary results of the paper by directly running the codes and using the pre-processed data provided by the authors. The performance on average accuracies over 60 rounds and the corresponding boxplots were evaluated by comparing Interboost and the other methods. Furthermore, we additionally used logistic regression as a baseline classifier for both datasets. Moreover, besides the confusion matrix for LM, the confusion matrices for UIUC, which was not shown in the paper, was also produced by us. Our findings are listed as follows:
1. Interboost yielded accuracies of 86.2% and 81.7% on LM and UIUC dataset respectively, which was 2.5% and 2.3% lower than the accuracies reported in the paper. 
2. The performance of Interboost was better than Bagging, which was consistent with the original paper. However, in contrast to the findings in the paper, the reproduced results indicated that the accuracies of Interboost is lower than that of Adaboost by 1.1% in the LM dataset and 0.8% in the UIUC dataset, and were only 0.1% higher than that of FC in both datasets. 
3. Surprisingly, logistic regression yielded the best performance on accuracy for both datasets among all the methods. The accuracies were 2.8% and 1.6% higher than those of Interboost for LM and UIUC dataset respectively. 
4.  For both datasets, the boxplot of Interboost was slightly more compact than that of FC, however, it was less compact than that of Bagging and Interboost.  
5. In the confusion matrices for LM dataset, similar to the paper, the two networks looked complementary. The overall accuracies produced by us was 83.13% and 84.13% by the two base networks, and achieved 87.25% by Interboost. Our empirical results confirmed the pattern described in the original paper, although our evidence was weaker than the paper in claiming the complementary behavior of the two base networks.
6. In the confusion matrices for UIUC dataset, the overall accuracy by Interboost (80.51%) was again higher than that of the two networks (74.63% and 79.97%). However, the complementary behavior of the two base networks was less evident in this dataset, as neither of them was an `` "expert"in classifying croquet, polo and rock-climbing. In particular, the accuracies of croquet were only 64% by the first base network and 42% by the second base network, jointly resulting in accuracy of 52% for croquet by Interboost. Our additional results implied that the complementary performance of the two base networks possibly could not be generalized to all datasets.

we also developed the codes for re-implementing the algorithm of Interboost by ourselves. The average accuracies  was 86.6% and 81.8% on LM and UIUC dataset respectively, which was 2.1% and 2.2% lower than the accuracies reported in the paper. This is very close to the results we obtained when we ran the code provided by the authors. Again, the boxplot of Interboost did not seem to reveal its superiority in variability over the other methods for both datasets. 
Overall, the proposed methods had good prediction performance, although part of our results were not entirely consistent with the paper. Our results indicated some randomness of the performance by Interboost, and thus further investigation was needed. We do not really have explanations about why we have obtained slightly worse performance than the authors, as we used exactly the same hyperparameters as the paper. Moreover, all the results from the authors and us were based on the average accuracies over 60 runs. We suspected that this was simply due to variance resulted from the weights initialization. Running the methods over more runs rather than only 60 runs might provide more robust conclusion.

content.title: Reproducibility of the paper's results
content.comment:
The paper proposes a method that ensemble two base (weak) neural networks (NN) to tackle the problem of classification when the number of samples for training is limited. The main contribution of this method is the weighting of examples inside of the loss function for each NN. For each training sample, there are two different and complementary weight values W1 and W2 (W1+W2=1, 0 < W1, W2 <1), one for each loss function. These weights are updated iteratively after a specific number of epochs, according to classification results using a validation data set. The aim is to make of each NN an expert of the classification of a different group of samples, therefore making the ensemble result the union of the results of the individual classifiers.

Dealing with a small number of data points while avoiding overfitting and poor generalization is the main objective of this work which seems promising. The presented results in the paper tend to show that the proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art ensembling methods such as AdaBoost and SnapShot. We tried to reproduce the work done by the authors and came to the following conclusions.

First, using the code and data set provided by the authors, the obtained results do not seem to be exactly the same as those reported in the paper. This might be due to the random initialization of the sample weights and the weights of the networks with a seed that was not given. However, we could see that the ensemble accuracy is actually better in terms of bias and variance than the results of the individuals NN classifiers for the two data sets (LM and UIUC).

When comparing the results obtained with the state-of-the-art methods, we found that on average the proposed method slightly outperforms SnapShot, but its variance is relatively bigger. This might be explained by the fact that the proposed method has a greater number of variables randomly initialized than Snapshot, making the method more susceptible to fall in local minimums. A better initialization method of these variables could possibly improve the results of the proposed method.

Concerning the paper itself, apart from the fact that it is well written and easily understandable, we found that some important details are missing, which leads to some confusion for the reader. For instance, the caption of the second figure gives two different ways to update the sample weights. The first equation uses p1 as nominator while the second one uses p2. After some analysis, we understand that it is both because of the logarithm function and the expected complementarity between p1 and p2, but more explanations would be helpful.

Some questions still seem unanswered by the paper. Here is a short list of questions for which we would have like to find answers in the paper.
How does it compare to a classical CNN approach? That is using the CNN to also predict and not only do features extraction. How does it compare to CNN methods designed to deal with small datasets?
This method creates more parameters to learn and makes the solution space bigger. Can the solving be optimized? How does it scale to bigger datasets?

Link to full review: https://drive.google.com/open?id=1aeM3EuFlc9aWVplRsPvqIk7Z1Sacq8Sg

content.title: Reproducibility Study of InterBoost
content.comment:
In this study we investigate the reproducibility of the InterBoost method as proposed in an ICLR 2018 conference submission, Interactive Boosting of Neural Networks for Small-Sample Image Classification. Reproducibility is being examined as a way to promote research integrity, identify areas in the research that may need attention or clarification, and encourage the authors to be as transparent as possible. We attempt to reproduce the experiments and results stated by the authors of the paper, in which they describe the merits of a new ensemble learning method called InterBoost. The main purpose of InterBoost is to improve the performance of neural networks on small-sample training datasets while reducing variances; the datasets used in the paper are the LabelMe and UIUC sports datasets.
Our goal is to analyze the authors’ process and determine areas that can be improved in terms of creating a reproducible experiment. To do so, we require a reproducibility framework specific to the paper in question. We begin by reviewing the material provided by the author, i.e. the original paper and the supplementary code. Next, we determine if the results of our experiment match the claims of the paper. Finally, we examine how well InterBoost translates to larger networks as this will determine if the method is truly significant, or if it only applies to circumstances in the paper.
Our preliminary finding was that the code for all baseline models in the repository provided by the authors did not run without making some adjustments, even when using the recommended versions of Python, TensorFlow, and Keras. For example, some of the code for baseline models like AdaBoost would call weight files that did not exist in the repository. Others, like Bagging and FC were initially loading models with functions that led to array shape errors when fitting the models. The correct functions for loading models were included in the repository and the code was easily fixed, but in order to make each baseline experiment more easily reproducible we suggest the authors modify their code to allow users to run the exact baseline experiments described in the paper without any extra changes.
The code provided for InterBoost had no errors, but upon running the code we found that 180 instances of InterBoost training for 8 iterations of 100 training epochs gave an average accuracy of 86.7% for LM and 81.8% for UIUC, consistently lower than the results reported in the paper for both LM and UIUC datasets by at least 2%, making it on par with several of the other baselines. We also found that the polynomial SVM baseline consistently scored 8.6% higher than the results reported in the paper for LabelMe, and 30.9% higher than the results reported for UIUC and, as a result, SVM achieves the best performance among all tested models in all experiments.
We also ran experiments on FC, Bagging, AdaBoost, Snapshot, and InterBoost with a training set reduced by 50 samples for each class, as described in the paper. Except for Snapshot, our results were far greater than those reported in the paper with InterBoost achieving 82.8% for LM and 77.9% for UIUC instead of the reported 80.2% and 77.9%. In our results, InterBoost was comparable to the FC base model, which achieved 82.9% for LM and 77% for UIUC, and AdaBoost, which achieved 83.1% for LM and 76.4% for UIUC.
When expanding the base model to five networks, we found similar results. On the LabelMe dataset, InterBoost scored 84.7%, while the AdaBoost baseline scored 86.4%. On the UIUC dataset, InterBoost scored 80.5%, while the AdaBoost baseline scored 81.1%.
Based on these facts, we conclude that we cannot reproduce the main results of this paper. The code was analyzed thoroughly to make sure it matched the methods described in the paper and we assume that the code provided is the authors’ final version. However, it is possible that the authors did not post the final version of their code, which could explain our lower observed results for InterBoost. Should the repository not contain the most recent version of the authors’ code which yields these better results, we recommend that the authors update their code and make any necessary fixes. If the code in the repository is indeed correct, we recommend that the authors provide greater detail on the steps taken to achieve their results. Should one like to learn more about our reproducibility study, it is available at https://goo.gl/NJaf6P

display_title: A Replication Study of "INTERACTIVE BOOSTING OF NEURAL NETWORKS FOR SMALL-SAMPLE IMAGE CLASSIFICATION"

content.title: A Replication Study of "INTERACTIVE BOOSTING OF NEURAL NETWORKS FOR SMALL-SAMPLE IMAGE CLASSIFICATION"
content.comment:
The paper proposed a method 'InterBoost' to improve accuracy of neural network on small-sample image classification task. The author did a great job on executing and comparing the proposed method with a good number of other image classification methods. InterBoost is introduced as a ensemble method, therefore author focused on comparison with other ensemble methods, such as Bagging, Adaboost and Snapshot. There are two datasets used for test and validation: LM and UIUC sporting datasets. These two datasets are suitable for this study, since they are both small in size for training neural network classifiers. The author later on extended validation to include results using even smaller datasets. This is achieved by using a fraction of the dataset when training the networks. It is greatly appreciated that the author provided source code with the paper. It not only helped illustrating concept of algorithm, but also higher reproducibility of the study.

With some modifications to the source code provided, we were given a good hand to understand the proposed algorithm. However, there are some challenges we have encountered in the process of trying to reproduce the reported result.

The main challenge is that the paper does not include a comprehensive description of the parameter values used in the training process, such as learning rate and loss function used. Considering the paper is primarily focus on introducing the ensemble method, parameters of the underline neural network training is not decisive as long as parameter values are identical across all methods. After all, these parameters are exposed in the source code, where reviewers are provided access to. Although some parameters used in the underline neural network without specification caused minor effect to us, important parameters to some of the ensemble methods such as learning rate in Snapshot not specified in the paper brought some challenges to our replicate work. For the latter type of missing parameters values, we had to make some guesses based on our own interpretation from the text. This may lead to potential result differences between our reproduced work and the reported result stated in the paper. As a consequence, Snapshot outperformed the other ensemble methods in our reproduced work. Snapshot is also the one that we had to embed our own interpretation into the algorithm, because the parameters used for this specific method are not specified in text and there is no source code provided for Snapshot.It would be great if readers can be provided with a more comprehensive description of each test for better reproducing precision.

The authors first used VGG convolutional neural network to extract features as a data pre-processing step. The features are then loaded into the fully connected neural network(FC) for network training. Although FC was used as the base network for all ensemble methods in the paper, the authors didn't provide clear explanation why FC architecture was specifically selected by the paper.Moreover, convolutional neural network(CNN) is best known for its superior performance at image classification and thus should be a very good baseline method for comparison with InterBoost in the paper. However, it is unclear why CNN is not included it in their experiments. Even though training algorithm is illustrated in steps in the paper, it would be great if the author can also discuss about the mathematical intuition behind it.

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
We are grateful to all the reviewers for their valuable and constructive suggestions and comments. The suggestions of studying more baseline methods and conducting more theoretical and experimental work are useful input for us to enhance our work. Several reproducibility studies helped us identify some errors in the published code and in the experimental process, which we unfortunately were unaware of. We highly value the importance of scientific rigor and decide to withdraw the manuscript from ICLR 2018. Our detailed response letter can be found at https://goo.gl/9PG3V5

Best regards,
The authors
